Surah "The Jinn"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, to your community:

﴿It has been revealed to me that﴾ — that the matter and the case — they agreed on opening the hamza of "annahu" (that it), because it is the deputy subject (nā'ib fā'il) of "ūḥiya" (it was revealed), and "an law istaqāmū" (that if they had gone straight), and "anna al-masājida" (that the mosques), by way of conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "annahu istamaʿa" (that he listened). So "an" is a lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy one (al-thaqīla), and "an qad abligū" (that they have indeed conveyed), because "yaʿlamu" (he knows) transitively governs it. And they read it with a kasra after the fā' of the consequent (fā' al-jazā'), and after the verb of saying (al-qawl), such as: "fa-inna lahu nāra jahannam" (then indeed for him is the fire of Hell), and "qālū innā samiʿnā" (they said: indeed we have heard), because it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) quoted after a verb of saying. They differed regarding the opening and the kasra of the hamza in "annahu taʿālā jaddu rabbinā" (that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord), down to "wa-annā minnā al-muslimūn" (and that among us are the Muslims). Ibn ʿĀmir and the Kufans except Abū Bakr opened it, by way of conjunction upon "annahu istamaʿa" (that he listened), or upon the place (maḥall) of the prepositional phrase in "āmannā bihi" (we believed in him), its estimate being: "wa-ṣaddaqnāhu, wa-ṣaddaqnā annahu taʿālā jaddu rabbinā, wa-annahu kāna yaqūlu safīhunā..." (and we affirmed him, and we affirmed that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, and that our foolish one used to say...), to its end. Others read it with a kasra, by way of conjunction upon "innā samiʿnā" (we have heard), and they pause at the ends of the verses.

﴿A group of the jinn listened﴾, a company (nafar), from three to ten,

﴿from the jinn﴾, the jinn of Nasibin,

﴿and said﴾, to their people, when they returned to them from listening to the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ during the dawn prayer,

﴿Indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾, marvellous, unique, unlike all other books in the beauty of its composition and the soundness of its meanings. And "ʿajab" (wonder) is that which is outside the habitual; it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) placed in the position of the adjective "ʿajīb" (wondrous).

﷿ "He guides to rectitude" (yahdi ila al-rushd): He calls to what is correct, or to tawhid (affirming God's oneness) and faith.

﴿So we believed in it﴾: in the Qur'an. Since believing in it is believing in God and in His oneness, and disavowal of association (shirk), they said: ﴿and we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾ of His creation. It is also permissible for the pronoun in "bihi" (in it) to refer to God (exalted is He), because His saying "our Lord" (bi-rabbina) explains it.

And [it is] that exalted is the majesty (jadd) of our Lord, ﴿and that He—exalted is He—[has the] majesty of our Lord﴾... 

Let me translate precisely as the text stands:

﴿And that He, exalted is He, the majesty (jadd) of our Lord﴾, i.e., His greatness. It is said: "Such-and-such became majestic (jadda) in my eyes," meaning he became great (ʿaẓuma). From this is the saying of ʿUmar—or Anas: "When a man recited al-Baqarah and Al ʿImran, he became majestic (jadda) among us," meaning he became great in our eyes.

﴿He has not taken a companion﴾, i.e., a wife.

﴿Nor a son﴾, as the unbelievers among the jinn and mankind say.

"And that our foolish one [safihuna] used to say about Allah an extravagance [shatatan]" — Tafsir of verse 72:4.

Here is the translation:

﴿And that our foolish one used to say﴾, meaning our ignorant one, or Iblis, since there is no one more foolish than him (for he is the foolishest of all),

﴿about Allah an extravagance﴾, meaning disbelief, because of its remoteness from the correct position. It is derived from "shattat al-dar," meaning the house became distant, i.e., far away. Or it means a statement that deviates from the truth, which is the attribution of a consort and a son to Him. And "al-shatat" is exceeding the limit in wrongdoing and other things.

And we had thought that mankind and jinn would never speak a lie against God. ﴿And we had thought that mankind and jinn would never speak a lie against God﴾, [the word "كذبا" is] "a lie" as a verbal noun (qawlan kadhiban), or "a thing lied about" (maktudhan fihi), or it is in the accusative as an infinitive (ala al-masdar), since lying is a type of speaking. That is: it was in our opinion that no one would lie against God by attributing to Him a consort and a son, so we used to believe them in what they attributed to Him, until the Qur'an made clear to us their lie.

It was the custom of a man of the Arabs, when he alighted in a frightening place of the land, to say: "I seek refuge with the lord (sayyid) of this valley from the foolish ones of his people," meaning the greatest of the jinn. Then (the Qur'an) said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verse 6:

﴿And indeed there were men among mankind who sought refuge with men among the jinn, so they increased them in ﴾ — that is: mankind increased the jinn by their seeking refuge with them, ﴿rahaqan﴾ — transgression, folly and arrogance, by saying: "We have become masters of the jinn and mankind." Or: the jinn increased mankind ﴿rahaqan﴾ — sin, because of their seeking refuge with them. The origin of "al-rahaq" (ar-rahaq, the overwhelming of what is forbidden; i.e., the act of coming upon what is prohibited) is ghashayan al-mahdhur.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verse 7:

﴿And that they﴾, and that the jinn,

﴿thought as you thought﴾, O people of Makkah,

﴿that Allah would never raise anyone up﴾, after death. That is, the jinn used to deny the resurrection, as you deny it. Then, upon hearing the Qur'an, they were guided and acknowledged the resurrection, so why do you not acknowledge it as they did?

And that we touched the heaven, but found it filled with a strong guard and shooting stars.

Hmm, let me translate faithfully and completely, as instructed:

"And that we touched the heaven" (﴿وَأنّا لَمَسْنا السَماءَ﴾): we sought to reach the heaven and to listen to the speech of its inhabitants. "Al-lams" (اَللَّمْسُ) means "al-mass" (اَلْمَسُّ, touching), so it was used metaphorically for "seeking," because the one who touches is a seeker and one who tries to learn.

"We found it filled with a strong guard" (﴿فَوَجَدْناها مُلِئَتْ حَرَسًا شَدِيدًا﴾): a group of strong angels who guard. "Harasan" is the plural of "ḥāris" (حارِسٌ, guard), and it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz). It was also said that "al-haras" (اَلْحَرَسُ) is a singular noun meaning "al-ḥurrās" (اَلْحُرّاسُ, the guards), like "al-khadam" (اَلْخَدَمُ) meaning "al-khuddām" (اَلْخُدّامُ, the servants). This is why it is described as "shadīdan" (شَدِيدًا, strong, singular). Had one looked at its meaning, it would have been said "shidādan" (شِدادًا, strong, plural).

"And shooting stars" (﴿وَشُهُبًا﴾): the plural of "shihāb" (شِهابٌ), meaning shining stars (كَواكِبَ مُضِيئَةً).

﴿And indeed we used to sit in some of its places,﴾ of the heaven, before this,

﴿[in order] to listen,﴾ to the hearing of the news of the heaven. That is to say: we used to find some parts of the heaven free of the guards and the meteors before the mission (al-mab'ath).

﴿Whoever now tries to listen,﴾ wishes to listen, after the mission,

﴿will find for himself﴾ for himself,

﴿a watching flame (shihaban rasadan).﴾ This is an attribute of "shihaban," in the sense of "al-rasid" (the watcher): that is, he will find a flame watching over him and lying in wait for him. Or it is a collective noun for "al-rasid," in the sense of "possessors of flames who watch with stoning," and they are the angels who pelt them with the meteors and prevent them from listening. The majority hold that this did not happen before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). It has been said that stoning occurred in the Jahiliyyah, but the devils used to steal hearing at certain times, and then they were entirely prevented from stealing after the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verse 10:

﴿And indeed we do not know whether evil is intended for those upon the earth﴾, [i.e.] a punishment,

﴿or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾, [i.e.] good and mercy.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verse 11:

﴿And among us are the righteous (al-ṣāliḥūn)﴾: al-abrār (the pious), al-muttaqūn (the God-fearing).

﴿And among us are﴾: a people,

﴿beneath that﴾: here the described noun (al-mawṣūf) is elided. They are those who are moderate in righteousness, not fully perfect in it; or they intended "those who are not righteous" (ghayr al-ṣāliḥīn).

﴿We were divided into diverse paths﴾: an explanation of the division mentioned, i.e., we were people of varied schools (madhāhib mutafarriqa) or of differing religions (adyān mukhtalifa). "Al-qidad" is the plural of "qidda," which is a piece, from "qadadtu al-sayr," meaning I cut the leather strip.

"And that we thought" — we were certain (ayqanna),

"that we would never cause Allah to fail" — we would never escape Him (lan nafutahu),

"in the earth" — a circumstantial phrase (hal); that is: we would never cause Him to fail while being in the earth, wherever we might be upon it,

"and we would never cause Him to fail by fleeing" — a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial phrase; that is: nor would we cause Him to fail by fleeing from it to the sky. And this is the attribute of the jinn, and of their states and beliefs.

"And indeed, when we heard the guidance," — the Qur'an — "we believed in it," — in the Qur'an, and in Allah — "so whoever believes in his Lord, then he does not fear" — "then he does not fear" is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar) — "a diminishing" — a reduction from his reward — "nor any burden" — i.e., neither will humiliation overtake him, from His saying: "and humiliation will overtake them" [Yunus: 27], and His saying: "and neither darkness nor humiliation will cover their faces" [Yunus: 26]. And in this there is evidence that deeds are not part of faith.

"And among us are the Muslims (al-muslimun), the believers,

and among us are the unjust (al-qasitun), the disbelievers, who deviate from the way of truth. "Qasata" means he acted unjustly (jara), and "aqsata" means he acted justly (adala),

"Then whoever has submitted, those have sought out right guidance" (fa-man aslama fa-ula'ika tahharaw rashadan): they sought guidance. And "al-taharri" means seeking what is most fitting (al-ahra), i.e., what is best (al-aula).

"And as for the deviators (al-qasitun), they have been, in the knowledge of Allah,

﴿fuel for Hell﴾, i.e., kindling (wuqud). In this is evidence that the disbelieving jinn will be punished in the Fire, while the manner of their reward is left in suspense (yutawaqqaf)."

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verse 16:**

﴿And that﴾: it is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy (thaqilah) particle, meaning "and that He (innahu)." It is part of what was revealed, i.e., "it was revealed to me that the matter..."

﴿If they had remained steadfast﴾: i.e., the ones who deviate from the truth (al-qasitun),

﴿upon the way﴾: the way of Islam,

﴿We would have given them to drink of abundant water﴾: much (ghadaqan), and the meaning is: We would have widened provision for them. He mentioned water in abundance because it is the cause of abundance of provision.

(p-552) ﴿That We may test them therein﴾: that We may try them, to see how they give thanks for what they have been granted.

﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord﴾: from the Qur'an, or from the Tawhid (Oneness of God), or from worship.

﴿He will make him enter⁠﴾ — with the yaʾ (in the verb yasluk), which is the reading of the Iraqi (Kufan) readers other than Abu ʿAmr — meaning: He will cause him to enter.

﴿a punishment ever-increasing (ʿadhaban ṣaʿadan)⁠﴾: harsh, difficult. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of ṣaʿida, one says: ṣaʿida ṣaʿadan and ṣuʿudan. The punishment is described by it because it overwhelms the one being punished (yatasaʿʿadu al-muʿadhdhab), i.e., it rises over him and overpowers him, so he cannot bear it. From this is the saying of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Nothing has weighed on me (tasaʿʿadanī) as much as the proposal of marriage (khuṭbat al-nikāḥ)," meaning: nothing has been as hard on me as that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verse 18:

﴿And that the mosques belong to God﴾, is part of what was revealed; i.e., it was revealed to me that the mosques—that is, the buildings constructed for prayer in them—belong to God. It was also said: its meaning is, "And because the mosques belong to God, do not call upon anyone," with the lām connected to "do not call upon" (lā tadʿū). That is: ﴿So do not call upon anyone alongside God﴾, in the mosques, because they are exclusively for God and for His worship. It was also said: "the mosques" (al-masājid) means the members of prostration (aʿḍāʾ al-sujūd), which are: the forehead, the two hands, the two knees, and the two feet.

And that when the servant of Allah (Abdullah), Muhammad (ﷺ), stood up to prayer, [the jinn heard him],

Its implied construction: "And it was revealed to me that when the servant of Allah stood up..."

[Who] calls upon Him, that is, worships Him and recites the Qur'an. He did not say "the Prophet of Allah" or "His Messenger," because "servant" is among the most beloved names to the Prophet (ﷺ), and because, since it occurred in the Prophet's (ﷺ) own speech about himself, it was phrased in the manner that humility requires. Or, because the worship of the servant of Allah to Allah is not something unusual, such that they would be "almost upon him as a mass" (labadan).

"They were almost" (kadu): the jinn almost...

"Upon him as a mass" (labadan): groups, the plural of "lubdah" (a tuft or heap), out of wonder at what they saw of his worship, the following of his companions after him, and admiration for what he recited of the Qur'an, because they saw what they had never seen the like of.

﴿Say: "Indeed I only call upon my Lord﴾, alone, "قالَ" (qāla, meaning "he said"), "other than ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah,"

﴿and I do not associate anyone with Him﴾, in worship. So why do you wonder at me and crowd upon me?!

Say: "Indeed, I do not control for you any harm" (ḍarran), meaning harm (maḍarrah),

"or any right guidance" (rashadan), meaning benefit (naf'an). Or he meant by ḍurr (harm) misguidance (al-ghayy), as evidenced by the reading of Ubayy: "ghayyan wa-la rashadan" (misguidance and not right guidance). That means: "I am not able to harm you, nor to benefit you, because the one who harms and the one who benefits is Allah."

(p-553) ﴿Say: Indeed, no one will protect me from Allah,﴾ meaning: no one will repel His punishment from me if I disobey Him, like the saying of Salih, peace be upon him: ﴿Who will help me against Allah if I disobey Him?﴾ [Hud: 63]. ﴿And I will not find, other than Him, any refuge,﴾ i.e., any place of refuge (mulタjaʾ) to turn to.

﴿إلا بَلاغًا مِنَ اللهِ﴾ [Except a message from Allah]: this is an exception (istithna') from "لا أمْلِكُ" (lā amliku, "I do not possess"). That is, "I possess neither harm nor guidance for you, except a message from Allah." And "﴿قُلْ إنِّي لَنْ يُجِيرَنِي﴾" [Say: "Surely none will protect me from Allah"] is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad), to affirm the negation of ability from himself and to show his own helplessness. It has been said that "بَلاغًا" (balaghan) is a substitute (badal) for "مُلْتَحَدًا" (multaḥadan), meaning: "I will not find any refuge apart from Him, except that I convey from Him what He sent me with." That is: "Nothing will save me except that I convey from Allah what I have been sent with, for that will save me." Al-Farra' said: "This is a conditional clause with its response (shart wa-jaza'), and it is not an exception. And "إنْ" (in) is separated from "لا" (lā), and its underlying form is: "إنْ لا أُبَلِّغْ بَلاغًا" (in lā uballigh balāghan), meaning: "If I do not convey, I will not find any refuge or protector for myself apart from Him," like your saying: "إنْ لا قِيامًا فَقُعُودًا" (in lā qiyāman fa-qu'ūdan, "If not standing, then sitting"). And "البَلاغ" (al-balāgh), in these aspects, means "التَّبْلِيغ" (al-tablīgh, the conveying).

﴿وَرِسالاتِهِ﴾ [and His messages]: this is a coordination (ʿaṭf) on "بَلاغًا" (balāghan), as if it were said: "I possess nothing for you except conveying and the messages," that is: "except that I convey from Allah, saying: Allah said such-and-such, attributing my words to Him, and that I convey His message with which He sent me, without addition or subtraction." And "مِن" (min) is not a complement (ṣilah) of "التَبْلِيغ" (al-tablīgh), because one says "بَلَّغَ عَنْهُ" (ballagha ʿanhu, he conveyed from him). Rather, it has the function of "مِن" in ﴿بَراءَةٌ مِنَ اللهِ﴾ [Tawba 9:1: a disavowal from Allah], that is: "a message existing from Allah."

﴿وَمَن يَعْصِ اللهَ ورَسُولَهُ﴾ [And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger]: in refusing to accept what was revealed to the Messenger, because it is mentioned immediately after the conveying of the message.

﴿فَإنَّ لَهُ نارَ جَهَنَّمَ خالِدِينَ فِيها أبَدًا﴾ [then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever]: He used the singular in His saying "لَهُ" (lahu) and the plural in "خالِدِينَ" (khālidīna), in accordance with the wording of "مَن" (man) and its meaning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verse 24:

﴿Hatta﴾ (until) is connected to an omitted element, which the context indicates. It is as if it were said: "They will continue in what they are upon until ﴿when they see what they are promised﴾, of the punishment,

﴿then they will know﴾, at the time the punishment descends upon them,

﴿who is weaker in helper and fewer in number﴾, they or the believers?" That is: the disbelievers will have no helper on that Day, while the believer will be helped by Allah, His angels, and His prophets, peace be upon them.

(p-554) "Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will appoint for it a distant term." I do not know (ma adri): I do not know.

"Whether what you are promised is near": of the punishment.

"Or whether my Lord will appoint for it" — with the ya' vowelled with a fatha (yaftah al-ya'): read by the Hijazi reciters and Abu 'Amr.

"A distant term" (amadan): an extremely distant limit. Meaning: you will certainly be punished, but I do not know whether it is imminent or deferred to a appointed time.

Translation:

﴿He is the Knower of the unseen﴾: it is the predicate of an implied subject (mubtada'), i.e., He is the Knower of the unseen.

﴿So He does not disclose﴾: so He does not make known

﴿His unseen to anyone﴾: from among His creation.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verse 27:

﴿Except whom He has approved of the messengers﴾: except a messenger whom He has approved, for the knowledge of part of the unseen, so that his report of the unseen would be a miracle (mu'jizah) for him, for He informs him of His unseen what He wills. And "of the messengers" is an explanation of "whom He has approved." When a walī (saint) reports something and it then comes to pass, he is not certain about it, but he reported on the basis of his dream, or by firasah (intuitive insight), on the principle that every karamah (miraculous favour) of a walī is a miracle of the Messenger.

It is mentioned in al-Ta'wilat: Some of them said: "In this verse there is an indication of the refutation of the munajjimah (astrologers), but this is not so, for among them are those whose reports come true. Likewise the mutatayyibah (those who deal in perfumes and remedies), who know the natures of plants, and this is not known by reflection alone. It is thus known that they came to this knowledge through a messenger whose trace has ended, and whose knowledge remained among the creation."

﴿Then indeed He sends forth﴾: He causes to enter,

﴿from before him﴾: before the Messenger,

﴿and from behind him a guard﴾: guardians from among the angels, who protect him from the devils, safeguard him from their whisperings and their confusions, until the revelation is conveyed.

Translation of the passage:

﴿That He may know﴾, Allah, 

﴿that they have indeed conveyed﴾, i.e., the Messengers, 

﴿the messages of their Lord﴾, complete, without addition or deficiency, to those to whom they were sent. That is: that Allah may know that this exists, in the state of its existence, just as He knew before its existence that it would exist. He made the pronoun in "from before him" (min bayni yadayhi) singular, in agreement with the word "man" (من) in form, and He made the verb in "they have conveyed" (ablaghu) plural, in agreement with its meaning.

﴿And He encompasses﴾, Allah, 

﴿what is with them﴾, i.e., the knowledge that is with the Messengers.

﴿And He has enumerated everything in number﴾, of the drops of rain, the sand, the leaves of trees, and the foam of the seas. So how could He not encompass what is with the Messengers of His revelation and His speech?! "Adadan" (عددًا) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: and He knew every thing counted and limited; or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the sense of "iḥṣā’an" (إحصاءً).
